Edo period

The Edo period, also called the Tokugawa period, is the period between 1600 or 1603 and 1868 in the history of Japan, when the country was under the rule of the Tokugawa shogunate and some 300 regional daimyo, or feudal lords.

Emerging from the chaos of the Sengoku period, the Edo period was characterized by prolonged peace and stability, urbanization and economic growth, strict social order, isolationist foreign policies, and popular enjoyment of arts and culture.
In 1600, Tokugawa Ieyasu prevailed at the Battle of Sekigahara and set up hegemony over most of Japan, and in 1603 was given the title shogun by Emperor Go-Yōzei.

Ieyasu resigned two years later in favor of his son Hidetada, but maintained power, and defeated the primary rival to his authority, Toyotomi Hideyori, at the Siege of Osaka in 1615 before his death the next year.
From 1635, daimyō had to spend alternating years in the capital Edo, where their family was required to reside permanently, in a system of "alternate attendance" in order to keep the daimyō in check.
By 1639, all foreigners were expelled under the policy of sakoku, with the exception of Dutch traders on the island of Dejima in Nagasaki, beginning a period of isolation.
Japanese scholars developed schools of neo-Confucian philosophy, and samurai, now mostly employed as administrators, formalized their bushido code of morality.
In 1853, Japan was forcibly opened to Western trade by United States Commodore Matthew C.
The Edo period came to an end in 1868 with the Meiji Restoration and the Boshin War, which restored imperial rule to Japan.
Instrumental in the rise of the new bakufu was Tokugawa Ieyasu, the main beneficiary of the achievements of Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi.
Already a powerful daimyo (feudal lord), Ieyasu profited by his transfer to the rich Kantō area.

Ieyasu's victory over the western daimyo at the Battle of Sekigahara (21 October 1600, or in the old Japanese calendar, on the 15th day of the ninth month of the fifth year of the Keichō era) gave him control of all Japan.
After Hideyoshi's death, Ieyasu moved quickly to seize control of the Toyotomi clan.
After further strengthening his power base, Ieyasu installed his son Hidetada (1579–1632) as shōgun and himself as retired shōgun in 1605.
Ieyasu still failed to achieve complete control of the western daimyo, but his assumption of the title of shōgun helped consolidate the alliance system.

The Tokugawa became more powerful during their first century of rule: land redistribution gave them nearly seven million koku, control of the most important cities, and a land assessment system reaping great revenues.
There were twenty-three daimyo on the borders of Tokugawa lands, all directly related to Ieyasu.
The Tokugawa shogunate not only consolidated their control over a reunified Japan, but also had unprecedented power over the emperor, the court, all daimyo, and the religious orders.
To ensure a close tie between the imperial clan and the Tokugawa family, Ieyasu's granddaughter was made an imperial consort in 1619.
At the top of this hierarchy sat the Rōjū (Senior Councilors), a council that rotated monthly duties to direct foreign policy, manage relations with the lords, and oversee national security.
Specific administrative sectors—such as finance, religious affairs, or the management of major cities like Edo, Kyoto, and Nagasaki—were the responsibility of officials called Bugyō (Commissioners).
To maintain order and detect dissent, the Metsuke (Inspectors) operated as an internal intelligence network.
The Hyōjōsho (Supreme Court) served as the highest judicial body for disputes between domains.
Historians refer to the Tokugawa system as "parcellized sovereignty" because there was no unified national treasury, national tax code, or national judiciary.
The Tokugawa helped the imperial family recapture its old glory by rebuilding its palaces and granting it new lands.
Instead, it operated as a network of reciprocal duties called yaku: the Shogunate provided security and peace, while the domains offered loyalty and service when required.
A code of laws (Buke shohatto) was set up to regulate the daimyo houses.
The various regulations and levies not only strengthened the Tokugawa but also depleted the wealth of the daimyo, thus weakening their threat to the central administration.
While the Shogun exercised hegemonic control over the nation, the daimyo had full administrative control over their territory and their complex systems of retainers, bureaucrats, and commoners.
Large domains like Tosa or Satsuma were nearly independent states with their own armies, legal codes, tax systems and paper currency within their borders.
A lord from a domain like Tosa might travel with nearly 3,000 retainers, hundreds of horses, and dozens of boats.
To acquire cash for their journeys and capital stays, domains shipped their surplus tax rice and local specialties to Osaka, which became the national commodity market.
Under the leadership of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the government sought to replace the era of chaotic piracy (wakō) with a structured, profitable system of organized trade.

The devalued price of gold in Japan was one immediate, enormous effect.

In the final years of the Tokugawas, foreign contact increased as more concessions were granted.
The Harris Treaty, forced on the bakufu in 1858, secured the privilege of Americans to reside and travel in a limited number of areas.
The treaty also banned the opium trade, set up extremely low tariffs favorable to American merchants, and guaranteed extraterritoriality for American citizens in Japan.
Tokugawa Nariaki opposed the signing of the new treaty, and Hotta, lacking the support of key daimyo, sought imperial sanction.

The court officials, perceiving the weakness of the bakufu, rejected Hotta's request and thus suddenly embroiled Kyoto and the emperor in Japan's internal politics for the first time in many centuries.
When the shōgun died without an heir, Nariaki appealed to the court for support of his own son, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, for shōgun, a candidate favored by the shinpan and tozama daimyo.
Recently some scholars have suggested that there were more events that spurred this opening of Japan.
Yoshimune, eighth Tokugawa shōgun from 1716 to 1745, started the first Kyōhō reforms in an attempt to gain more revenue for the government.
In 1767 to 1786 Tanuma Okitsugu also initiated some unorthodox economic reforms to expand government income.
Similarly, Matsudaira Sadanobu launched the Kansei Reforms in 1787–1793 to stabilize rice prices, cut government costs, and increase revenues.
The final economic reform of the Tenpō era of 1841–1843 had similar objectives.

Fort Smith Trolley Museum
The Fort Smith Trolley Museum is a streetcar and railroad museum in Fort Smith, in the U.S.
The museum opened in 1985, and operation of its streetcar line began in 1991.

The first museum building was constructed in 1985, on former Missouri Pacific Railroad land, and purchases and donations of property in the 1990s allowed activities and storage to expand onto adjacent parcels.
Four vehicles in its collection, a streetcar and three steam locomotives, are listed on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP).

The now approximately three-quarters-mile-long (1.2 km) streetcar line also passes four NRHP-listed sites, including the Fort Smith National Historic Site, the Fort Smith National Cemetery, the West Garrison Avenue Historic District and the 1907 Atkinson-Williams Warehouse Building, which now houses the Fort Smith Museum of History.
The Fort Smith Trolley Museum (FSTM) opened to the public in 1985, and trolley/streetcar operation began in 1991.
In the first seven months of operation, though the end of 1991 (in which five months had daily operation), more than 10,000 rides were given.
The initial line was about one-quarter mile long, using ex-Frisco freight tracks, along which FSSRA volunteers had installed trolley wire and support poles.
The first extension was opened by the city's mayor on October 9, 1994, and took the line to the gates of the Fort Smith National Cemetery.
At the line's west end, an extension of the track and wires to Garrison Avenue, the town's main street, opened on August 29, 1996.

The first extension since 1996 was opened on November 24, 2002, starting with a curve just before the previous terminus at Garrison between 3rd and 4th streets and running along the south side of Garrison Avenue, to 2nd Street.
At the other end of the line, a very short extension in May 2005 took the track across Wheeler Avenue to a new terminus at 7th Street, making the line about 3,000 feet (900 m) in length.
The line's first extension since 2005 opened on May 21, 2016, bringing into use newly laid track and trolley wire along 7th Street.
The line's new eastern terminus is on 7th Street at Rogers Avenue, and the approximately 750-foot extension made the full line about 0.75 miles (1.2 km) long.

Køge Bay (Danish: Køge Bugt) is an approximately 500 square kilometres (190 sq mi) shallow Danish bay in the southern part of Øresund, between the Greater Copenhagen area in the North (or more precisely the southernmost peak of Amager) and Stevns Klint in the South, and as a part of Zealand.
The area around the bay's shores are built-up from Copenhagen to Køge, including Copenhagen suburban areas like Brøndby Strand, Vallensbæk, Ishøj, Hundige, Jersie and others.
Due to its closeness to the Baltic Sea, the average surface salinity is lower than elsewhere in Øresund, especially when compared to the northern parts of this sound.
The landing approaches Copenhagen Airport runways 04L and 04R goes over the bay, it is used for approximately 30% of all landings.
1 July 1677, a sea battle between a Dano-Norwegian and a slightly larger Swedish fleet occurred in the bay.
An indecisive battle between a Dano-Norwegian fleet and Sweden was fought in 1710.
In August 2017, Swedish journalist Kim Wall was murdered in the bay by entrepeuner Peter Madsen on board his submarine UC3 Nautilus.

Greenwood was arrested in 2018, as was Konstantin Ignatov in March 2019.

2017–18 La Liga
The 2017–18 La Liga season, also called LaLiga Santander for sponsorship reasons, was the 87th since its establishment.
The season began on 18 August 2017 and concluded on 20 May 2018.
Barcelona, under new manager Ernesto Valverde, won the league title on 29 April 2018 with four matches to spare.
Levante, Girona, and Getafe were the newly promoted clubs competing in the season, with Girona entering La Liga for the first time in its history.
At the end of the season, Málaga, Las Palmas, and Deportivo La Coruña were all relegated to the Segunda División.
In the transfer window, Barcelona were involved in the new world record transfer, selling Brazilian forward Neymar to French club Paris Saint-Germain for €222 million.

Barcelona first topped the table on 16 September after winning 5–0 in its third match of the season against neighbours Espanyol, eventually making a run of seven wins from the start of the season that ended with a 1–1 draw at Atlético Madrid.

Valencia improved on its previous campaign and began its new season well, with Marcelino getting the best out of players such as Italian striker Simone Zaza and on-loan Portuguese winger Gonçalo Guedes.
Real Madrid struggled in the first half of the season, with problems including a smaller squad, injuries and the comparatively poorer goalscoring form of Cristiano Ronaldo relative to recent seasons.

In January 2018, Barcelona added to its attack by spending €160 million on Brazilian Philippe Coutinho from Liverpool, while the end of a transfer ban allowed Atlético to register Diego Costa and Vitolo for action.
Málaga were the first team to be relegated, ending its ten-season stay in La Liga with its descent confirmed after a 0–1 loss against Levante on 19 April.
Three days later, Las Palmas' relegation was also confirmed after the Canarian team lost 0–4 at home to Alavés to end its three-year top flight status.
On 29 April, Barcelona sealed its 25th league title with a 4–2 win at Deportivo La Coruña, with Lionel Messi scoring a hat-trick.
Barcelona still had four matches to play, and it was the second part of its double, having earlier won the 2018 Copa del Rey Final.
The result also made Deportivo the final of the three relegated teams, sending them back to Segunda División for the first time in four years.
A day later, Real Betis, under new manager Quique Setién, booked its entry to the UEFA Europa League following a 2–1 win over Málaga.
In its second-last match of the season, Sevilla drew 2–2 with city rivals Betis to confirm seventh place and qualification for the UEFA Europa League at the expense of Getafe.
Levante was the first team from Segunda División to achieve promotion, after a one-year absence from La Liga, on 29 April 2017 after winning 1–0 against Oviedo.
Girona were promoted as the runners-up after drawing 0–0 against Zaragoza on 4 June 2017; this was its first promotion to the top division.
Getafe was the last to be promoted after defeating Huesca and Tenerife in the play-offs, one year after its relegation.
The three promoted clubs replaced Sporting Gijón, Osasuna and Granada, which were relegated at the end of the previous season, ending their top flight spells of two, one and six years respectively.
Real Betis completed their stadium renovation and it was grown to 60,720 seats, becoming the fourth biggest stadium in Spain.
Meanwhile, after their first promotion ever to La Liga, Girona expanded Estadi Montilivi temporarily for hosting 13,450 spectators.

Barcelona were on track to complete the first unbeaten La Liga season since the Spanish Civil War (and first in a 38-match season), but surprisingly lost its 37th match 4–5 at Levante, having only conceded 24 goals all season to that point.

The initial fanfare – titled "Sunrise" in the composer's programme notes – became well known after its use in Stanley Kubrick's 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey.

"Of the Backworldsmen" begins with cellos, double-basses and organ pedal before changing into a lyrical passage for the entire section.
"Of the Great Longing" introduces motifs that are more chromatic in nature.
"Of Joys and Passions", in C minor, marks the first subject theme of the work's allegro (exposition) proper.
The strings prevail in "The Song of the Grave", in which some would say the second subject theme, in B minor, starts.
"Of Science and Learning" features an unusual fugue beginning at measure 201 in the double-basses and cellos, which consists of all twelve notes of the chromatic scale.

The end of the "Song of the Night Wanderer" leaves the piece half-resolved, with high flutes, piccolos and violins playing a B major chord, while the lower strings pluck a C.
One of the major compositional themes of the piece is the contrast between the keys of B major, representing humanity, and C major, representing the universe.
The tone-poem ends enigmatically in two keys, the Nature-motif plucked softly, by the basses in its original key of C—and above the woodwinds, in the key of B major.
The unsolvable end of the universe: for Strauss was not pacified by Nietzsche's solution.

Ancient Tombs at Longtou Mountain
The Ancient Tombs at Longtou Mountain are the burial sites of twelve royal figures from the Balhae (Bohai) kingdom.
The discovery of Princess Chŏnghyo's tombstone resolved speculation amongst scholars that the area was the former location of Hyundeok Province (顯德府) of the Balhae Kingdom.
The cemetery was in use until the end of the Balhae Kingdom.
The site has been a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level since January 13, 1988.
In 1982, the Yanbian Museum excavated seven tombs in the Dragon Sea area.
The inner north, east, and west walls were plastered, but the tomb had collapsed by 2012.
The mausoleum contains, among other things, the first complete discovered and detailed murals done by Balhae artists, and hence provides valuable insights to historians.
The mounds of earth lined with stones demonstrate the continuance of Goguryeo-style tomb but the formal clothing shows Tang style, which implies that Balhae actively accepted the Tang culture.
The murals displayed the image of the Balhae people in its completeness for the first time.

The burial chamber contains a 1.05-metre tall, 0.58-metre width × 0.26-m depth mugui-shaped (土圭) complete and unbroken granite epitaph, on which 728 Chinese characters, in the Regular Script style, are inscribed in 18 horizontal lines.
The Balhae scholar author of this epitaph was highly learned in the traditional Chinese literature, as reflected in the use of poetic lines modeled upon poets of the early Tang dynasty.
The epitaph shows that Balhae considered its ruler as an emperor equivalent to that of the Tang dynasty.

The epitaph is of a typical combined written form, which contained both the chronological writings of the Princess' whole life and the remembrance writings which displayed the praise and remembrance for the Princess.
The epitaph also recorded that the Princess died on Monday, 6 July 792, during the fifty-sixth year of the Daeheung era.
The gold ornament depicting a three stranded bird's wing is a piece of evidence demonstrating how Balhae was inherited of Goguryeo's crowns.
Only the pagoda's foundations remain, which show that it was originally square, measuring 5.50x5.65 m.
The burial chamber measured 2.10x3.10 m and was built from bricks, with stone slabs forming the roof.

Bamberg Symphony

The Bamberg Symphony (German: Bamberger Symphoniker – Bayerische Staatsphilharmonie) is a German professional orchestra that has resided in Bamberg since being set up in 1946 and regularly tours internationally.

The Bamberg Symphony was set up in 1946 by musicians who as a result of the Beneš decrees had been driven out of Bohemia, Moravia, the Czech Sudetenland as well as from German cities and had ended up in Bamberg.
The "core" of the orchestra comprised former members of the German Philharmonic Orchestra Prague.
The first concert of the orchestra was performed on March 20, 1946, in Bamberg.
The orchestra's musical roots trace back to Mahler and Mozart, and it is well known for its characteristic dark, full and resonant sound.

The Bamberg Symphony Orchestra is based in the Bamberg Concert Hall, which was opened in 1993 and acoustically optimized in 2008 by the Japanese acoustic designer Yasuhisa Toyota and has the nickname Sinfonie an der Regnitz (Symphony on the Regnitz).
2009 saw the concert hall undergo a comprehensive renovation and modernization following a concept by the designer Peter Schmidt.
The city's German theatre was also influenced by eminent artists such as Gustav Mahler.
After the German occupation, the orchestra was re-established as the German Philharmonic Orchestra Prague.
The musicians had to flee in May 1945 during the Prague uprising.
After the end of the Second World War, a number of top German-speaking musicians from Bohemia and Moravia arrived in Bamberg, after having been expelled by the Beneš decrees.
The majority of these musicians, roughly two thirds, were former members of the German Philharmonic Orchestra Prague, who formed the Bamberg Symphony Orchestra in 1946.
The first public concert was held under the name „Bamberger Tonkünstlerorchester“ before the orchestra was renamed ‘Bamberger Symphoniker’ shortly after.

The first conductors included Hans Schneider, Konrad Lechner, Hans Knappertsbusch, Herbert Albert, Georg Ludwig Jochum and finally Joseph Keilberth, who conducted his first concert in Bamberg in 1949.
In September 2016, Jakub Hrůša became the sixth Chief Conductor of the Bamberg Symphony, with an initial contract of four seasons.
In June 2018, the orchestra announced the extension of Hrůša's contract as its chief conductor through the 2025–2026 season.
In December 2023, the orchestra announced a further extension of Hrůša's contract as chief conductor through the 2028–2029 season.
From the very beginning, Keilberth's aim was to increase the number of radio recordings with the orchestra and to go on a tour in Germany and abroad.

During the Keilberth era, numerous renowned guest conductors were invited to conduct the „Bamberger“, including Eugen Jochum, Hans Rosbaud, Fritz Lehmann, Georg Solti, Clemens Krauss, Lovro von Matačić, Heinrich Hollreiser, Robert Heger, André Cluytens, Heinz Wallberg.
The great concert hall of the Bamberg Concert and Congress Hall, which has been home to the Bamberg Symphony since 1993, is named after Joseph Keilberth.
In 1971, Jochum took over the position of Chief Conductor, and from 1973 he remained in close contact with the orchestra as a guest conductor.
On the occasion of his 76th birthday, the Bamberg Symphony awarded Jochum the title of Honorary Conductor in November 1978.
As Jochum's successor, the Hungarian István Kertész was introduced, but died in a swimming accident on the beach in Tel Aviv a few months before taking up his post, on 16 April 1973.
On 1 April 1977, the Scotsman James Loughran finally introduced himself to the Bamberg Symphony as guest conductor.
On 4 February 1984, Loughran conducted his last concert with the Bamberg Symphony and the collaboration ended by mutual agreement on 31 August 1983.
The Polish conductor Witold Rowicki took over as interim artistic director until his successor took office.

Colin Lawson
Colin James Lawson (born 24 July 1949) is a British clarinettist, scholar, and broadcaster.
A pupil of Thea King, Lawson was a member of the National Youth Orchestra of Great Britain during his teenage years.
Postgraduate studies in music at the University of Birmingham saw Lawson awarded an MA in 1972 for his study of the clarinet in eighteenth-century repertoire.
His pioneering doctoral research into the chalumeau was completed at the University of Aberdeen in 1976.
In 2000, in recognition of his work across theory and practice, Lawson received a DMus from the University of London.
In 2015, celebrating Lawson's pre-eminence in performance studies, the University of Sheffield awarded him an HonDMus.
In December 2025 Lawson was awarded an HonDMus by the Royal College of Music.
Following academic positions in Aberdeen and Sheffield, Lawson was appointed to the Chair of Performance Studies at Goldsmiths, University of London in 1998.
Between 2001 and 2005 he was Pro-Vice Chancellor and Dean of the London College of Music & Media at Thames Valley University (now the University of West London).
Between July 2005 and August 2024 he was Director of the Royal College of Music, London.
His extensive discography comprises concertos by Fasch, Hook, Mahon, Mozart, Spohr, Telemann, Vivaldi and Weber, as well as a considerable variety of chamber and orchestral music.
Among more recent recordings are two discs of sonatas by Xavier Lefèvre and a highly acclaimed CD of the Mozart Clarinet Quintet and other fragments.
Lawson has an especially close association with Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto K622, which he performs regularly on both modern and historical instruments.

Lawson’s Cambridge Handbook to Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto (1996) examines the work’s genesis, composition and construction, as well as the career of the dedicatee Anton Stadler and his innovative basset clarinet.
In addition to directing performances of the work, he has played it in collaboration with conductors such as Roy Goodman, Christopher Hogwood, Roger Norrington and Joshua Rifkin.
His first monograph, The Chalumeau in Eighteenth-Century Music, was published in 1981 by UMI Research Press, and remains the most extensive study of the instrument and its repertoire.

Amongst later publications for Cambridge University Press are The Cambridge Companion to the Clarinet (1995), a Cambridge Handbook to Brahms’s Clarinet Quintet (1998) and The Cambridge Companion to the Orchestra (2003).

With Robin Stowell he initiated the series of Cambridge Handbooks to the Historical Performance of Music, including their joint introductory volume (1999) as well as his own volume on the early clarinet (2000).
The Cambridge History of Musical Performance edited by Lawson and Stowell was published in February 2012.
Their most recent volume, The Cambridge Encyclopedia of Historical Performance in Music, was published in September 2018.
In 2019 the volume was recognised as an "outstanding work of music reference", winning IAML's C.B.
His most recent publication is the jointly edited volume for Routledge entitled Inside the Contemporary Conservatoire: Perspectives from the Royal College of Music, London.
In the Queen's 2016 Birthday Honours Lawson was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) for services to music and music education.

The East End Historic District encompasses a large 19th-century residential area in eastern Galveston, Texas.
The area is roughly bounded by Broadway to the south, Market St to the north, 19th St to the west, and 9th street to the east.

After the Texas Republic was set up in 1836, Galveston Island was developed as the republic's principal port.
Its street network was platted in 1838, and by 1850 it was the second largest port on the Gulf Coast (after New Orleans).
The eastern end of Galveston Island became its preeminent residential district, where the city's civic and business leaders built their houses.
Wilbur Cherry, an early newspaper published in the city, built a house on Cherry Street in 1852 which is one of the district's oldest.
The grandest mansion in the area is the so-called Bishop's Palace, completed in 1893 for politician and lawyer Walter Gresham.
Most of the district's 550-plus buildings are residences that show Victorian architectural styles, although a number of relatively unaltered examples of the Greek Revival survive from its early days.
The East End was protected as a local historic district in 1970.
Historically, The East End was a hub of the Black community and institutions.

José Carrillo de Albornoz, 1st Duke of Montemar
José Carrillo de Albornoz y Montiel, 1st Duke of Montemar (8 October 1671 – 26 June 1747) was a Spanish Army officer and nobleman who served as the viceroy of Sicily from 1734 to 1737.
During the War of the Spanish Succession he aligned with the side of Philip of Anjou and fought as mariscal de campo in the Battle of Villaviciosa (1710) in the cavalry under the Count of Aguilar.
In 1731 he headed the expeditionary force that occupied the Duchy of Parma for its legal heir, Don Carlos, future King Charles III of Spain.
In 1732 Blas de Lezo led the Spanish navy and Montemar the Spanish army in retaking Oran and Mazalquivir from the Turks (which had taken both cities in 1708.
His greatest victory was the Battle of Bitonto on 25 May 1734, which sealed Spanish control of Naples.
For this victory, the king Philip V of Spain ennobled him as the first Duke of Montemar.
In 1741 he was appointed as head of the 50,000 men strong expeditionary Spanish army in Italy during the War of Austrian Succession.

Colonna started his career in Italian armies of Spain during the last Italian War, becoming a feudal lord in Naples.
In 1548, he was summoned to serve as a page to Prince Philip, and in May 1552, he married Felicia Orsini as part of a potential reconciliation between his parents.

Following that campaign, he used Spanish military force to seize his father's lands, exiling Ascanio to the Abruzzo region, where the latter was subsequently arrested by the viceroy on suspicion of treason.
The following year, he was moved to the troops of Cosimo I de' Medici, a Spanish ally, and participated in the campaign to wrest Siena from French control.
In August, he played a pivotal role in the cavalry during the Battle of Marciano under the command of Gian Giacomo Medici a conflict that resulted in the destruction of the Franco-Sienese army.
A few months later, his father lodged a complaint against him with Pope Julius III, though nothing came of it.
By 1555, Colonna was a cavalry officer in the tercios of Naples and acquired his father's estates of Tagliacozzo and Paliano thanks to the intercession of Prince Philip.
Colonna escaped to Paliano, although his mother, his wife, and Cardinal Guido Sforza were all placed under house arrest.
Realizing the stronghold was ill-defended against papal troops, Colonna returned to the Viceroyalty of Naples and reunited with his imprisoned father, though relations between them stayed strained.

At the end of the year, Giovanna and Felicia managed to escape and reunite with him in Naples, provoking the wrath of the pontiff, who excommunicated him in May 1556 and confiscated his lands for his own nephew, Giovanni Caraffa.
The resumption of hostilities in July allowed Colonna to exact his revenge.
In 1557, he defeated Giulio Orsini in a major battle at Acuto, and soon after achieved a victory at Valmontone by outmaneuvering French commander Francis of Guise.

Colonna made a triumphal entry into Rome, where Paul IV died shortly thereafter amidst mobs that mutilated his statue, and saw the pontiff replaced by Pius IV.

Furthermore, he would henceforth work alongside the Popes to achieve religious unity in Italy, and ideally across the rest of Europe, in opposition to the Ottoman Empire.

In 1569, he traveled to Spain, proposing to be sent as reinforcements against the Dutch Revolt, ideally as governor of Milan so as to maintain the "Spanish Road".

In March 1570, despite holding the office of Grand Constable of Naples, a position that entailed obligations to Philip II, Colonna participated without royal authorization at the ceremony where Pope Pius V invested Cosimo I de' Medici as Grand Duke.
The presence of Paolo Orsini, a member of a traditionally pro-French family, even led the king to suspect that Colonna was involved in a conspiracy against him.
In the summer of 1570, Pius appointed him Captain General of the papal fleet, yet another controversial decision, as Colonna once again accepted the post without consulting Philip.
His role would be significant and demanding of strong leadership, given that the Pope had not possessed a fleet of his own since the papal navy was wiped out at the Battle of Djerba in 1560.
Venice had promised to provide a flotilla of twelve galleys to the Pope in exchange for forming a league against the Ottomans, so Colonna was sent to take command.

Ultimately, the monarch gave his approval after being persuaded to join by Juan de Zúñiga, and he sent Giovanni Andrea Doria with a Spanish-Genoese fleet to reinforce Colonna, subject to certain conditions.
A similar situation unfolded in the Venetian Senate, who had wanted a Venetian commander for the league, although they too reluctantly accepted the appointment.
Colonna seized the opportunity to visit Venice and attempt to improve relations with the Republic, whether out of shared interest or personal ambition.
Colonna’s participation in the first campaign, aimed at relieving the siege of Nicosia, began under promising auspices.
The Venetians even assigned him as his flagship the quinquereme built by Vettore Fausto as the very first galleass.

Upon rendezvousing with Doria and the Venetian Girolamo Zane in Candia, it was agreed that Colonna would lead the League while deferring to Doria, who possessed the most maritime experience of the three, yet this arrangement failed to resolve the inevitable disagreements.

Colonna, supported by Zane and the Spanish captain Álvaro de Bazán, advocated for attacking the Turkish fleet while it was still scattered along the coast of Cyprus, arguing that there was still time for operations before the onset of autumn weather.
By the time they reached Cyprus, they learned that Nicosia had already fallen.
Disagreements intensified to the point where the Spaniards wished to withdraw from the campaign, and Colonna and Zane had to press them to stay.
Colonna clashed openly with Doria, and Carlo d'Avalos of the Spanish fleet nearly came to blows with the Roman.
Ultimately, the fleets decided to return to Candia, where the alliance completely disintegrated, and the campaign ended with the coalition forces returning empty-handed.
To make matters worse, Colonna encountered a storm between Corfu and Ancona that sank the greater part of the papal flotilla, leaving him to return home with only four galleys.
For his part, Doria came to fear that Colonna and Bazán would form a political front against him.

In August of that same year, joined by his cousin Pompeo, Colonna assembled his fleet at Messina alongside those of Don John and the Venetian Sebastiano Venier, in preparation for the upcoming campaign.
His diplomatic skills were once again evident, as he persuaded the Venetians to agree to embark Spanish marine infantry onto their galleys, which were otherwise poorly equipped and undermanned.

During the ensuing Battle of Lepanto on October 7, 1571, Colonna served with distinction.He commanded the papal Capitana (flagship) as part of the Centre division, where he rescued the Real, flagship of commander Don John of Austria.
When the Real was almost taken by the Ottoman janissaries, Colonna came alongside, with the bow of his galley and mounted a counter-attack.
With the help of Colonna, the Turks were pushed off the Real and the Ottoman flagship of Ali Pasha was boarded and swept.
The entire crew of Ali Pasha's flagship was killed, including the commander himself.
In the process, Colonna was shot twice in the chest and suffered a damaged hand, although he survived the engagement and was subsequently praised by Don John of Austria for his efforts.
On his return to Rome to announce the victory, a ceremony modeled on ancient Roman triumphs was held, featuring chariots, parades, and chained captives.
Among the captives was Said Bey, the surviving son of Ali Pasha, whom Colonna handed over to Pius V to be released soon after.
In June, albeit with a reduced force, Colonna sailed with part of the squadrons to Messina, where forces were once again gathering for a planned campaign against the Turkish coast.
Colonna thus set sail for Corfu with these ships, serving as acting general.
When the surviving Ottoman admiral, Occhiali, put to sea in June with 200 galleys, Colonna took command of the League fleet and moved to Morea to block his path to Venice.

The second encounter of the skirmish took place days later off Cape Matapan, where Uluj retreated with his left flank battered.
Once clear of the Turks, Colonna pressed to rendezvous with John of Austria and Bazán before the Ottomans could ambush their much smaller fleet.
Once reunited, John of Austria reprimanded them for having engaged Occhiali under dangerous conditions, so Colonna and Andrade offered their resignations, but Don John refused to accept them.
Before undertaking the siege of Navarino, Colonna once again mediated between the Spanish and the Venetians.
The Venetian Giacomo Foscarini flatly refused to embark Spanish soldiers; Colonna managed to embark Papal troops instead and then replaced them with Spanish soldiers on his own ships.

1979 Boston University strike
The 1979 Boston University strike was a labor strike involving employees at Boston University, a private university in Boston, Massachusetts, United States.
The strike was participated by faculty members, clerical workers, and librarians, which began on April 5 up to April 23.
The changes and regulations implemented under the presidency of John Silber, who became president of the university in 1971, were the major reasons behind the strike.
Silber initially challenged the legality of the union, but by 1978, a court ruling mandated that the university had to commence negotiations with the union.
In early 1979, the union began preparing for strike action, and on April 5, following a disagreement over a tentative agreement that had previously been reached, the union went on strike.
The strike resulted in the cancellation of several hundred classes and particularly affected the College of Liberal Arts.

On April 14, the faculty voted to end the strike after the university agreed to the previous tentative agreement, with the provision that they not perform any sort of sympathy strike with other unions.
For this reason, historian Gary Zabel calls the strike a Pyrrhic victory for the faculty.
Silber had previously worked at the University of Texas at Austin, where he had set up a reputation as a New Deal liberal.
By 1976, the faculty senate for BU voted 377–117 in a vote of no confidence, asking Silber to resign, as did eight members of the BU board of trustees.

In particular, Silber pushed for departments to hire friends of his at an inflated pay and vetoed some recommendations for academic tenure, particularly for professors who had expressed a left-leaning political stance.

In 1967, the first labor union representing professors at a bachelor degree granting college was set up as a local union of the American Federation of Teachers at what is now the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth.
By 1975, dozens of universities and over 200 two-year colleges were unionized, representing approximately 15 percent of all professors in the United States.

Shortly after BU-AAUP held its representation election, these workers formed the Boston University Staff Organizing Committee, which consisted of about 800 clerical workers.

Both of these unions had held representation elections of their own by 1979, but the university refused to negotiate with them and instead filed legal action wherein they questioned the legitimacy of the elections.

The union and university were primarily at odds with regards to pay increases, highlighted by a letter released by a trustee in January 1979 that read, "More than anything else, we seek tranquility on campus.
By March, the union had reduced this amount to 14 percent for the first year and two smaller amounts for the next two years of the contract, but the two sides remained at an impasse.

As part of the agreement (which was solidified with a public handshaking between Silber and negotiators), both side's bargaining units would present the agreements for deliberation amongst their respective sides for a maximum of 72 hours before a straightforward yea or nay vote.
The previous day, Silber had held a closed-doors meeting at the Algonquin Club with several prominent members of the board.

Although disbanded in 1919 following the end of hostilities, it was re-raised in 1921 in the Citizens Force (later called the Militia) as a part-time infantry battalion based in Victoria.

During the Second World War, the 7th Battalion served primarily in a garrison role, firstly being used to defend the Australian mainland before deploying late in the war to take part in the Bougainville campaign in 1944–1945.
On Bougainville, as part of the 23rd Brigade, they took part in the fighting in the central sector of the island in the last months of the war.
In 1948, the battalion was re-raised as an amalgamated unit with the 8th Battalion when the Citizens Military Force was reformed.

While this force would draw from the military forces that already existed—the part-time Citizens Force and the Permanent Military Force—it would be largely be made up from recruits not currently serving.
Known as the Australian Imperial Force (AIF), initially it was to consist of 20,000 men, comprising one infantry division and a light horse brigade.
Recruitment for the first intake began on 10 August 1914, and the 7th Battalion was among the first units raised, forming less than a fortnight after the declaration of war.
Under the command of Lieutenant Colonel Harold Elliott, the battalion was brigaded with the 5th, 6th and 8th Battalions to form the 2nd Brigade under Brigadier James Whiteside McCay.
In early April the battalion was moved to Alexandria and from there on to Lemnos Island.
On the morning of 25 April 1915, the battalion took part in the Landing at Anzac Cove, coming ashore as part of the second wave.
On 29 April, the 2nd Brigade was relieved by the 12th (Deal) Battalion and in early May the battalion was able to reorganise itself after its baptism of fire.
The respite did not last long, however, for only ten days after the landing at Anzac Cove, the 2nd Brigade was transferred to Cape Helles in order to take part in an attack on Krithia on 8 May 1915.

Nevertheless, they were involved in what is believed to be the first brigade-level attack conducted by an Australian force against an entrenched enemy and the attack earned the Victorians many plaudits.
In an effort to break this deadlock, the Allies launched an offensive in August and the battalion took part in the Battle of Lone Pine.
According to Ron Austin, during this fighting, the 7th Battalion lost 87 men killed; Arthur Dean and Eric Gutteridge give the total casualties as twelve out of fourteen officers and 680 Other Ranks.
Finally, in December the decision was made to evacuate the Allied force from the peninsula.

Upon arrival, the battalion was sent to the Somme, where its first major action came in July during the Battle of Pozières.
Throughout July and into August, the battalion was committed to the fighting twice, losing 55 men killed in the first battle and another 83 in the second.
In late August, the 7th Battalion, with a frontage equal to just over half its authorised strength, was transferred to Ypres, in Belgium, where they manned trenches near the Ypres–Commines canal.
On 30 September, the 7th Battalion, along with its sister battalion, the 8th Battalion, mounted a raid on the German line at Hollebeke with a force roughly equivalent to two platoons.
The raid was a great success, with the Australians overwhelming the defenders and capturing a section of the German line and killing up to 13 Germans, before withdrawing.
In October, the battalion returned to the Somme where they spent the winter months manning trenches and training.

In early 1917, precipitated by the loss of the high ground around Pozières, the Germans withdrew back to the Hindenburg Line in order to shorten their defensive line and to straighten a salient that had developed.

In February, the German withdrawal was discovered and the Allies, finding an open battlefield for the first time since 1914 and believing that the German Army was suffering from limited manpower, began an advance to follow them up.
On the night of 26/27 February, the 7th Battalion launched what was meant to be a trench raid, but turned into an open advance, seeing them extend their lines by 2.5 kilometres (1.6 mi).
The Allied advance, however, was brief as the Germans had set up themselves in strength, and was halted before the Australians reached Bullecourt.

Devolution in England
Devolution in England describes the process of the UK Government granting more powers to the subdivisions of England.
All of them, except the Greater London Authority, are groupings of local authorities in parts of England.
The concept of transferring powers to parts of England was first raised in 1912 by Winston Churchill, as part of his proposal for a federal system.

In the later half of the 20th century, concepts of provincial or regional governance were explored, with nine Government Office Regions created in 1994, and eight of them having regional chambers in 1998.
The lone exception, Greater London, had the devolved Greater London Authority set up in 2000 following a 1998 referendum.
Subsequently, the eight regional assemblies were abolished by 2010, and were followed by the introduction of the "combined authorities", with the first one set up in Greater Manchester in 2011.
From 2016, the role of a directly-elected mayor leading an authority was introduced, followed by a new form of body, a combined county authority, from 2023.
Since 2026, combined authorities, combined county authorities, and the Greater London Authority are all designated as a form of "strategic authority".
The mayoral strategic authorities sit on the Council of the Nations and Regions and the Mayoral Council for England.
The division of England into provinces or regions was explored by several post-Second World War royal commissions.
The Redcliffe-Maud Report of 1969 proposed devolving power from central government to eight provinces in England.
In 1998, the government of Tony Blair set up regional chambers for the eight regions of England outside of Greater London.
Following a successful referendum in 1998, a strategic regional authority was created for Greater London, the Greater London Authority (GLA).
The GLA was set up in 2000 and consists of a directly elected Mayor of London and an elected London Assembly.
Regional development agencies (RDAs) were set up in 1998 in all nine English regions.
In 2001, the government published a white paper proposing to reorganise the eight regional chambers into directly elected regional assemblies.
An "English Regions Network" was formed as a collective voice for England's eight regional chambers and the GLA.
In a white paper published in 2002, the government proposed decentralisation of power across England similar to that done for Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland in 1998.
An unsuccessful referendum on establishing an elected regional assembly in North East England took place in November 2004.
Regional chambers were phased out between 2008 and 2010, with some of their functions being assumed by Local authority leaders' boards.
The GLA is the only devolved area of England to remain from the old system of devolution to the nine English regions.
The 2009 Local Democracy, Economic Development and Construction Act provided the means for the creation of combined authorities, a type of strategic authority outside of Greater London.
Multiple combined authorities were created in the early-to-mid-2010s, The first combined authority was set up in Greater Manchester in 2011.
The Cities and Local Government Devolution Act 2016 was passed on 28 January 2016 and created an optional mayoral governance structure for the combined authorities.
The Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023 introduced an alternative type of strategic authority outside of Greater London, the combined county authority.
In 2013, the GLA set up the Devolution Working Group to oversee and further devolution in London.
In 2017 the work of these authorities along with Public Health England achieved a devolution agreement with the national government in regard to some healthcare services.
Under the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026, the Greater London Authority, combined authorities and combined county authorities were formally designated as strategic authorities.
Part 4 of act will establish the Local Audit Office, an independent body to oversee standards, registration of auditors and enforcement.
As of June 2026, there are twenty strategic authorities made up of thirteen combined authorities, six combined county authorities and the Greater London Authority.
All strategic authorities outside Greater London were voluntarily set up by their constituent councils.
In December 2024, the UK government published a white paper that outlined six strategic authorities to be created under the Devolution Priority Programme.

As of October 2024, 48% of the population and 26% of the land area of England is represented on the Mayoral Council.

No further action towards establishing an English Cabinet of Mayors was taken.

In 2022, Labour also proposed a similar body to be called the "Council of England", chaired by the prime minister and bringing together strategic authority mayors, representatives of local government and other stakeholders.

Beauval Indian Residential School (1895–1983) near the northern village of Beauval, Saskatchewan was a Canadian residential school operated by the Roman Catholic Church for First Nations children.
The school was on what is now the La Plonge 192 reserve across the Beaver River from Beauval.
La Plonge 192 is part of the English River Dene Nation and had 115 residents in 2011.
A fire on September 19–20, 1927, and an influenza epidemic in 1937 took the lives of many students.
In 1911 when Bishop Charlebois visited the school he wrote that all the 44 children there were taught both French and English but that the use of French dominated.
In 1927 there were 37 students in the school, 18 girls and 19 boys, when the wooden building was destroyed by fire.
In 1931 with the promise of a $75,000.00 grant from the Federal government a new school was started and was almost complete in January 1932.
